notes: Lesson defining algorithms and their properties. Hook: recipe analogy. Properties of algorithms (finite, definite, effective, input/output). Flowcharts. Pseudocode. Worked example: bubble sort trace. Video of sorting algorithms visualised. Class B complexity (18 units, 5 ECUs).

units.label: Hook: following a recipe as algorithm (text)
units.content_summary: A recipe is an algorithm: it is a step-by-step set of instructions that, if followed exactly, always produces the same result (a cake). This analogy introduces the concept of algorithms in everyday life before formalising it.

units.label: Recipe as flowchart (image)
units.content_summary: Simple flowchart for making toast: START → Insert bread → Push down toaster lever → Wait 2 minutes → [Is it toasted? No → Wait 30 seconds → loop; Yes] → Remove toast → Eat → END. Shows flowchart symbols and decision diamond.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: define an algorithm; list properties of a valid algorithm; represent algorithms using flowcharts and pseudocode; trace through a simple sorting algorithm; evaluate algorithmic efficiency.

units.label: Definition: algorithm (text)
units.content_summary: An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined instructions for solving a problem or accomplishing a task. Used in computing, mathematics, and everyday life. The word comes from the name of Persian mathematician Al-Khwarizmi (9th century).

units.label: Algorithm properties (text)
units.content_summary: Five properties of a valid algorithm: (1) Finiteness — must terminate in a finite number of steps; (2) Definiteness — each step must be precisely defined, no ambiguity; (3) Input — zero or more inputs from outside; (4) Output — one or more results produced; (5) Effectiveness — each step must be simple enough to be executed.

units.label: Flowchart symbols reference (image)
units.content_summary: Reference card showing standard flowchart symbols: oval (Start/End), rectangle (Process), diamond (Decision/Yes-No), parallelogram (Input/Output), arrow (Flow direction). Each symbol labeled and colour-coded.

units.label: Pseudocode introduction (text)
units.content_summary: Pseudocode is an informal, language-agnostic representation of an algorithm using English-like statements. More precise than plain English, less rigid than code. Keywords: INPUT, OUTPUT, IF/THEN/ELSE, WHILE/DO, FOR. Used to plan algorithms before coding.

units.label: Pseudocode example: find maximum (text)
units.content_summary: Pseudocode for finding the maximum of three numbers: INPUT a, b, c; IF a > b AND a > c THEN OUTPUT a; ELSE IF b > c THEN OUTPUT b; ELSE OUTPUT c; ENDIF. Shows structure and indentation conventions.

units.label: Bubble sort: algorithm description (text)
units.content_summary: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through a list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After each pass, the largest unsorted element 'bubbles' to the end. Repeated until no swaps needed. Simple but O(n²) — inefficient for large lists.

units.label: Bubble sort: trace table for [5,3,8,1] (image)
units.content_summary: Step-by-step trace table showing bubble sort on [5,3,8,1]: Pass 1: compare 5,3 → swap→[3,5,8,1]; compare 5,8 → no swap; compare 8,1 → swap→[3,5,1,8]. Pass 2: ...; Pass 3: sorted. Each comparison and swap explicitly shown.

units.label: Bubble sort pseudocode (text)
units.content_summary: Pseudocode for bubble sort: FOR i = 1 to n-1; FOR j = 1 to n-i; IF list[j] > list[j+1] THEN swap(list[j], list[j+1]); ENDIF; ENDFOR; ENDFOR. Nested loops shown with indentation.

units.label: Algorithmic efficiency: time complexity intro (text)
units.content_summary: Efficiency matters for large inputs. O(n) means time grows linearly with input size. O(n²) means time grows with the square — bubble sort is O(n²). O(log n) is very efficient (e.g. binary search). Brief introduction without full Big-O notation.

units.label: Efficiency comparison chart (image)
units.content_summary: Graph showing how execution time grows with input size n for O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), and O(n²). Lines diverge dramatically for large n, showing why efficient algorithms matter for real-world problems.

units.label: Video: sorting algorithms visualised (video)
units.content_summary: Visual comparison of sorting algorithms: bubble sort, insertion sort, merge sort, quick sort on bars of varying heights. Each bar animates as comparisons and swaps occur. Shows dramatically how faster algorithms reduce number of operations.

units.label: Real-world algorithms: search engines (text)
units.content_summary: Search engines like Google use complex ranking algorithms (PageRank) to sort billions of web pages by relevance in milliseconds. Algorithms also power: GPS navigation (shortest path), social media feeds (recommendation), fraud detection (pattern matching).

units.label: Practice problems (text)
units.content_summary: Five problems: identify whether a given procedure is a valid algorithm (check all 5 properties); draw flowchart for a given problem; write pseudocode for finding average of a list; trace bubble sort on given list; explain why efficiency matters for large inputs.
